metadata.purpose: Ep. 14 of the AI in Astronomy & Space Science series, from weekly_stem_videos/ideas.md Astronomy topic 14 (Star classification & spectra - AI reading stellar spectra to determine composition/age/distance faster than manual analysis). The episode takes COMPOSITION, because that is where the label-inheritance problem is cleanest and best documented; distance would need a second, unrelated mechanism.
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity palette. Terracotta #D97757 is the ONE accent and marks WHAT THE LABELS BROUGHT WITH THEM - the physics model in the chain, the error against truth, the inherited trend, the biased training set. Ink marks WHAT THE MODEL ITSELF DOES WELL - its agreement with its own labels, its repeat-measurement precision, and the anchored run that escapes the inheritance. The mapping never flips, so B05 teaches it once. Accented text is #A44A32; #B9B4A0 is strokes and fills only.
metadata.distinct_from_earlier_episodes: Eps. 01-06 had AI inspecting observations; 07 standing in for a calculation; 08 a division of labour; 09 an output that was never a measurement; 10 a training set produced by past decisions; 11 an objective that omitted the failure; 12 an evaluation inflated by the split; 13 a positive class that does not exist. Ep. 14 is the first where THE LABELS THEMSELVES ARE A MODEL'S OUTPUT. The data is real, the method is sound, the evaluation is honest, and the answer is still wrong - because 'ground truth' was never measured, it was computed. The limit is inherited rather than introduced, and it is invisible to every check performed against the same labels.
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00, B11, B12, B13. Every other beat illustrates its concept as a reel-local Manim scene (scenes.py). Plates come from assets/gen_stars.py, which runs the REAL algorithm - a quadratic data-driven model fitted per wavelength pixel and inverted at test time, exactly the published form - trained on labels from a physics pipeline carrying a deliberate temperature-dependent bias. THREE claims are ASSERTED and the script writes nothing if any fails. Seed 1414. B07 TRANSFORMS B06's scatter in place rather than presenting a second scatter plot, so the two beats do not read as consecutive slides. PUBLISHED (Ness et al. 2015; the SDSS DR14 documentation, which states the inheritance and the precision-is-not-accuracy point in the survey's own words) and COMPUTED-HERE are kept apart on screen and in the voice. No LaTeX/MathTex anywhere. metadata.channel_title is omitted for the GATE V edge-bleed reason logged in Ep. 03. scenes.py is ASPECT-AWARE.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about AI reading starlight to measure what stars are made of, and why its answers are more precise than they are true.

show.event: the composer types the ask on the cream stage
the send button arms in terracotta
running indicator: fitting 160 pixels
three result lines land in order

props.command: Data-driven models read stellar spectra and return temperature, gravity and composition, far faster than fitting physics. What are they actually trained on, and does the quoted precision mean the answer is right?
output: it has no physics in it - only the labels it was given
it agrees with those labels to 0.03 dex
against the truth: 0.13 dex, and the error is a straight line

beats.narration_text: Thirteen episodes of AI looking at the sky. This one is about where the right answers came from in the first place.

show.event: OM MALI writes in, terracotta hairline underlines it
role line fades in: Humanitarians AI - presenter
a card draws beside it
row one lands and is STRUCK: thirteen episodes / is the answer right
row two lands boxed: this one / where the answers came from
series line: Ep. 14 - the labels are a model's output

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea. Nobody hands the model real measurements of a star. It learns from labels that another model produced. So it does not predict the star. It predicts what that model would have said about the star.

show.event: a card draws on the cream stage
line one types: NOBODY MEASURES A STAR DIRECTLY, sub: the labels come from a physics model
line two: THE AI LEARNS THE LABELS, sub: and nothing else
line three lands in the accent and is UNDERLINED: SO IT PREDICTS THE MODEL
closer: not the star

beats.narration_text: This is real, and it works. The Cannon learned stellar parameters from five hundred and forty-two reference stars, then labelled fifty-six thousand. It uses no stellar physics at all. Only the labels.

show.event: a published-ledger chip lands: Ness et al., ApJ 2015
a small block of 542 marks draws in terracotta
a vastly larger field of 56,000 ink marks floods in beside it
a card types: no stellar models, no line list
closer: only the labels

beats.narration_text: Here is what it reads. Three stars, same temperature, same gravity, different amounts of metal. More metal, deeper lines. That relationship is everything the model learns, and it never learns why.

show.event: spectra.png fades in: three spectra stacked
the top one is named: fewest metals
the terracotta one is named: most metals
a dashed terracotta guide drops through ONE absorption line (pixel 47, the most metal-sensitive in the bank), visibly deeper in each spectrum down the stack
closer: it never learns why

beats.narration_text: But look at the chain. The star makes a spectrum. A physics model reads the spectrum and produces a number. The AI learns that number. Four links, and only the first one is nature.

show.event: a chain of four boxes draws left to right, one at a time
box one: the star
box two: the spectrum
box three lands in the accent: a physics model
box four: the data-driven model
a bracket closes under links two to four: not nature
closer: only the first one is nature

beats.narration_text: So I built it. Five hundred training stars, a real data-driven model, no physics in it at all. Against the labels it was trained on it agrees to three hundredths of a dex. That is the plot a paper shows.

show.event: agree.png fades in: predictions against the training labels
the one-to-one line is traced
axis labels land: what the model says, what the labels say
a counter lands: 0.03 dex
closer: this is the plot a paper shows

beats.narration_text: Now compare the same predictions to the truth, which in a simulation I happen to have. Same stars, same model, same spectra. Point one three dex. Four times worse than it looked.

show.event: the SAME scatter is still on screen from the beat before
the x-axis label swaps: the labels -> the truth
the points TRANSFORM in place and spread off the line
the counter rolls 0.03 -> 0.13 dex
closer: four times worse than it looked

beats.narration_text: And here is the number you would have quoted in the paper. Measure the same star twice, with fresh noise: the predictions scatter by eight thousandths of a dex. The real error is fifteen times that. The error bars describe neither.

show.event: bars.png: three bars on one axis
bar one is named: measure it twice, 0.008
bar two is named: agrees with its labels, 0.033
bar three rises far past both, in the accent: 0.128
a bracket spans bar one to bar three: 15x
closer: the error bars describe neither

beats.narration_text: And it is not scatter. Plot the error against temperature and it is a line, almost a perfect one. A bias shaped like astrophysics, which survives every check that compares averages.

show.event: structure.png: the error against temperature
the zero line is marked
the terracotta fit is already drawn in the plate and reads against the dashed zero rule
a counter lands: correlation 0.995
closer: a line, not a cloud

beats.narration_text: So the tell. Take away the teacher's bias and the error vanishes. Or anchor to a hundred and twenty stars measured a different way. Noisier labels, four times fewer, four times more accurate.

show.event: anchor.png: three bars of error against truth
the terracotta bar is named: 500 precise biased labels
the second bar is named: 120 noisy independent ones
the third, smallest: an unbiased teacher, the control
closer: fewer, noisier, and right

beats.narration_text: So: a data-driven model inherits its labels, and its error bars only measure how well it agrees with its teacher. Accuracy needs a number the teacher never touched.

show.event: the artefact page opens on the cream stage
line one lands
line two lands
line three lands
line four lands
line five lands in the accent

props.artifactTitle: What The Model Would Say - one page
artifactLines: A data-driven spectral model contains no physics - everything it knows arrives through its training labels.
Those labels are themselves the output of a physics model, so the student inherits the teacher's systematics.
It agreed with its labels to 0.03 dex and with the truth to 0.13 - and repeat measurements scattered by only 0.008.
The error was not scatter. Against temperature it was a straight line, correlation 0.995.
Anchoring to 120 stars measured a different way beat 500 precise but inherited ones.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Read it. Here is where my training labels came from. Tell me what they inherit from whatever produced them, and what I could measure a completely different way to check.
